27.0.0.en: We sail: it is understood from this that Luke accompanied Paul on this journey, and that he was also with him in Caesarea.

27.0.1.en: Augustan Regiment: it numbered 3,000 soldiers and was named after Caesar, and it served in duties attached to it.

27.0.2.en: Two years after Paul's arrest in Caesarea, Festus handed Paul and other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, to sail with them to Italy, where the capital Rome is, so that he might be tried there.

27.1.0.en: Paul and those with him boarded a ship of Adramyttium, named after the port of Adramyttium in western Asia (Turkey), and from there they would take another ship bound for Rome. With them was Aristarchus of Macedonia (northern Greece), specifically from the city of Thessalonica, the capital of the north. The presence of Aristarchus and Luke, Paul's two disciples, with him was a great comfort to him on this journey and a proof of their great love for him in bearing the dangers of the voyage.

27.2.0.en: Courteously: perhaps this was because of Festus' recommendation, and on the other hand because of the character of Julius, and also because of Paul's gentle and attractive personality and the fact that he was a Roman.

27.2.1.en: The ship arrived at Sidon, a Phoenician city (Lebanon), sixty-seven miles north of Caesarea. Julius treated Paul kindly and permitted him to visit his friends, that is, the Christians of Sidon, so that he might receive material and moral help from them, and perhaps he seized this opportunity to preach to them and strengthen their faith.

27.3.0.en: The voyage continued westward, and they sailed under the lee of Cyprus, so that it would shield them from the opposing westerly winds.

27.4.0.en: The ship passed by the provinces of Cilicia and Pamphylia in southern Asia (Turkey), then arrived at Myra of Lycia, which is the city of Myra in southern Turkey.

27.5.0.en: In the port of Myra of Lycia, they left the ship and boarded another one coming from Egypt, from the city of Alexandria, laden with grain (wheat) (v. 38) and bound for Rome. It was a large ship that carried a great number of passengers in addition to the quantities of grain in it.

27.6.0.en: The ship was a sailing ship, and because the wind was contrary, they sailed slowly until they came near the city of Cnidus in southern Turkey. Because of the force of the northwesterly winds, they could not advance westward, so they sailed south to the island of Crete until they reached its eastern tip, where the city of Salmone is. They moved with difficulty because of the intensity of the northwesterly winds, and they passed south of Crete, which shielded them to some extent from the violence of the winds, until they came to a place called Fair Havens (a city on the southern coast of the island of Crete, near the city of Lasea).

27.7.0.en: The fast: the fast of the Day of Atonement among the Jews, which falls on the tenth of the seventh Hebrew month, in the Feast of Atonement, which occurs in the autumn.

27.7.1.en: The Jewish fast of the Day of Atonement, which falls in the autumn, had passed, and the harsh winter weather had begun, and the northwesterly winds, opposed to their course to Rome, grew strong. So Paul, by God's guidance and from his previous experience in travel, warned them that sailing at that time would bring harm to the ship, the cargo, and the passengers themselves.

27.8.0.en: The ship's pilot and its owner thought that it was possible to sail to Italy, so the centurion obeyed them and disregarded Paul's opinion, considering them more expert in the sea than Paul, who was concerned with religious and literary studies.

27.9.0.en: Because the region of Fair Havens was not suitable for wintering in, they began to look for another harbor, away from the winds, in which to spend the winter. So they tried to head the ship toward the harbor of Phenice, forty miles to the west (that is, a three-hour sail), also on the south of Crete, since the island shields them to some extent from the northwesterly winds.

27.10.0.en: A gentle south wind blew, and the sailors felt that the weather was suitable for sailing. So they moved the ship westward toward the harbor of Phenice, keeping close to the island so that the winds would not pull them out into the sea and expose them to dangers.

27.10.1.en: God often sends us His counsel, but we rely on the opinion of the world and reject God's counsel and treat it lightly, and the grave consequences become proof of the error of our conduct. So do not resist the voice of God that you hear in the Church and from your father of confession and your spiritual guides, and do not rush into your decisions, but seek God's guidance so that you are not exposed to dangers.

27.11.0.en: After they had sailed a little, about five miles westward on their way to Phenice, a storm called Euroclydon, that is, the eastern waves in Greek, rushed upon them from the northeast.

27.12.0.en: The wind seized the ship out of the sailors' control, and they were unable to face the wind, so the passengers committed themselves into God's hand, and the wind carried them wherever it willed.

27.13.0.en: They passed by the island of Clauda, trying to haul in the boat used for carrying passengers from the shore to the ship, which they had been towing behind the ship because they were nearing Phenice. But when the winds seized them, they tried to lift the boat up into the ship so that the rope tying it to the ship would not break and the boat be lost or smashed. They succeeded in this, but only after great effort because of the violence of the winds.

27.14.0.en: To meet the storms, they began to undergird the ship with strong ropes so that the wind would not pull its planks apart and water fill it. They were near a gulf in North Africa called the Syrtis, and they feared that the winds would drive them into it because it was very shallow, so that if the ship entered it, it would run aground in its bottom and the winds would break it up. So they lowered the sails to lessen the effect of the winds on the ship.

27.15.1.en: The next day, because the winds grew stronger, they threw the ship's cargo of wheat into the sea to lighten it so that its escape would be easier.

27.16.0.en: On the third day they cast the ship's furniture into the sea to lighten it further.

27.17.0.en: The rays of the sun did not appear to them because of the thickness of the clouds, and likewise the stars at night. Since guidance for finding direction in those days was not by compass but by the sun in the day and the stars at night, they lost their bearings and despaired of being saved.

27.18.0.en: Because of seasickness and great fear, they abstained from food for a long time and their bodies grew weak. Then Paul stood among them and rebuked them for not obeying him when he warned them not to set sail from Fair Havens, which exposed them to these dangers. He said this not out of pride in his own opinion and dignity, but so that they would obey him in what he would say next.

27.19.0.en: Paul announced to them the good news that none of them would be drowned, but only the ship would be wrecked.

27.20.0.en: When Paul prayed to God, He sent His angel to him in the night that had passed.

27.21.0.en: The angel told Paul not to be afraid, because he would arrive safely in Rome and stand to be tried before Caesar, and that God would save all those who sailed in the ship from drowning for his sake.

27.21.1.en: Here we compare Paul, who by his obedience to God was the cause of the salvation of the ship's passengers, with the prophet Jonah, who by his disobedience to God was the cause of a predicament for the ship's passengers, until they threw him into the sea and it grew calm for them (Jonah 1:12).

27.22.0.en: Paul declared to them his confidence in the angel's word that they would be cast upon an island. Thus Paul's obedience saved them, after their disobedience had almost destroyed them.

27.22.1.en: Whenever we obey God, He becomes a protector for us against dangers and a covering over us. So obey God's commandments and the Church's guidance even if they are against your desires, because God knows what is good for you and loves you more than you love yourself. A person does what he is convinced of, but obedience is carrying out what one is not convinced of, so it is higher than everything, and its motive is love and faith in God.

27.23.2.en: Fourteen days had passed on the ship since it left the island of Crete, and most of this period was tormented by the winds and exposed to destruction in the Adriatic Sea, which lies between Italy and Greece. After that, it seems the sailors heard the sound of waves breaking on a shore, so they concluded that they were near some coast, because it was night and they could see nothing.

27.24.0.en: Fathom: the length of a man, that is, about 160 cm on average.

27.24.1.en: They used a rope with a weight at its end to measure the depth of the water down to the bottom, and they found the depth to be about thirty-six meters, because a fathom is about the length of a man. Then after a while they measured again and found that the depth had decreased and was only about twenty-four meters, so they were certain that their conclusion was correct.

27.25.0.en: Anchors: the plural of anchor, which is an iron shaft with an iron arc at its end, pointed on each side. This shaft is tied by a long rope to the ship, and when this anchor is cast onto the sea bottom, it digs into it and so holds the ship in its place. It was known among sailors by the name "al-Halb." Because it was midnight and visibility was nil, they feared that the shore might be rocky, so they cast four anchors from the stern of the ship to hold the ship in its place until daylight.

27.26.0.en: The sailors planned to escape from the ship to land by means of the boat, so they began lowering it into the sea, pretending that they would lay out more anchors from the bow of the ship to secure the vessel in its place. For if they had told the truth, that they would flee in this boat, which has room only for themselves, the centurion and the soldiers would have stopped them.

27.27.0.en: Paul warned the centurion and the soldiers about the sailors' attempt to flee in the boat, since that would lead to the passengers not being saved. For God's promise of their deliverance from drowning (v. 21) does not mean that they should cease their striving to reach land.

27.28.0.en: Then the soldiers cut the ropes from which the boat hung, and it fell and was lost in the sea.

27.29.0.en: During the remainder of the night, Paul began to urge everyone in great love to eat some food, because they had eaten nothing of value for fourteen days, whether because of seasickness or fear, which had exhausted their strength, a thing that would hinder their deliverance as God had promised them, that not a hair would perish from their heads.

27.29.1.en: Here Paul appears as a leader and guide for all the ship's passengers, although he was one of the prisoners. This is the fourth time that Paul concerned himself with leading those with him in order to save them from death (vv. 10, 21, 31).

27.30.0.en: Paul encouraged those with him to eat, by giving thanks to God, praying before them, and beginning to eat.

27.31.0.en: The hearts of the ship's passengers were reassured and they rejoiced at Paul's confidence in his God, and they ate. The number of all of them was two hundred and seventy-six.

27.31.1.en: The presence of the children of God in a place is a source of comfort, joy, and deliverance for those present, as the history of the Church records that because of Anba Paula, the first hermit, God sent down dew and rain upon the land of Egypt.

27.31.2.en: So know that God desires to bless everyone around you for your sake if you live with Him faithfully, and God awaits your prayer for all, that He may have mercy on them, because you are His child and your place is great in His heart.

27.32.0.en: For the first time in two weeks, the ship's passengers ate their fill. And since they knew that the ship was about to sink, they made a final attempt to save themselves by lightening the load, so they threw the wheat into the sea, hoping that this would help the ship come closer to the shore and shorten the distance that they would have to drag it to the shore.

27.33.0.en: When the light of day appeared through the thick clouds, they saw a bay in a land they did not know, so they agreed to steer the ship toward it, and the sailors did not know that this was the island of Malta, because they were far from its harbor (ch. 28:1).

27.34.0.en: They cut the ropes that tie the anchors to the ship, and likewise loosed the ropes that tie the rudder, and hoisted a sail to take advantage of the wind's thrust of the ship toward the shore.

27.35.0.en: Two seas: two opposing currents of water.

27.35.1.en: The ship entered a place between two water currents, whose collision causes sand to be deposited as a tongue of sand in the sea, in which ships run aground and cannot be moved. This is what happened to the ship when they brought it close to the shore. As the bow stuck fast in the sand and the waves began to strike violently against the stern of the ship, its planks began to come apart from one another, that is, the ship broke up.

27.36.0.en: Roman law punished a soldier with death if his prisoner escaped, so the soldiers thought of killing the prisoners.

27.37.0.en: The centurion did not agree with the soldiers' opinion, in order to save Paul, whom he loved and treated kindly, and whose wisdom he was convinced of, and God's work in him through his guidance of the ship's passengers. So he commanded those of them who were able to swim to go down into the water and head for the shore.

27.38.0.en: The rest, that is, those who could not swim, clung to boards and pieces of wood from the ship, and floated on them until they reached the shore, and so all were saved.

27.38.1.en: This was the fourth time that Paul escaped drowning, for he had been shipwrecked three times before (2 Cor 11:25).

27.38.2.en: The servant who has a clear purpose continues in his ministry however often obstacles recur, and so it was with Paul, because his calling and his election were firm. So do not be troubled by the obstacles that face you, for this does not mean that God has forsaken you, but continue in your spiritual striving and your service, trusting in the power of your God to rescue you, knowing that your sins do not hinder God's work with you as long as you repent of them.

28.0.0.en: The ship's passengers were at last saved from drowning in the sea and reached the island of Malta, which lies south of Italy, and they learned its name from its inhabitants.

28.1.0.en: The people of the island of Malta were not Romans, and the Romans call them barbarians. They were distinguished by generosity, and they kindled a fire to warm them, especially after their exposure to the severe cold that prevailed on the island at that time and the rain that accompanied it.

28.1.1.en: Thus God arranges care for His children wherever they are, according to the generosity of His giving, so that they may be free of care.

28.2.0.en: Paul was gathering dry sticks to make the fire burn more, and a viper came out from among them, having been hiding from the cold, and fastened on his hand.

28.3.0.en: Those who watched the Apostle Paul thought that every sin has a punishment, so they imagined that divine justice was pursuing him for a crime of murder he had committed, so that when he escaped drowning, it followed him with the serpent's bite.

28.4.0.en: Paul cast the serpent into the fire and suffered no harm from its bite.

28.5.0.en: The barbarians watched Paul, waiting for him to die by swelling from the effect of the poison or to fall down suddenly, and they waited a long time to no avail, so their thoughts about him changed and they supposed him to be a god, that is, immortal, unaffected by poisons and not dying.

28.5.1.en: People's opinion is constantly changing from the far right to the far left, and if a person tries to please them completely, he will lose his discipleship of Christ (Gal 1:10). So do not be concerned with pleasing people at the expense of the truth, and do not be disturbed by their accusations against you if you are not in error and are submissive to the Church, but be concerned to please them for God's sake, so that you may win their souls for Him.

28.6.0.en: The foremost man of the island and its governor, whose name was Publius, owned lands around the place to which they had escaped. The man received them as guests and treated them kindly for three days.

28.7.0.en: Publius' father was sick with a high fever and severe diarrhea (a bloody flux = dysentery), so Paul went in and prayed and laid his hands on him, and Christ healed him.

28.8.0.en: The news of Paul's healing of Publius' father spread on the island, so people brought their sick to him, and he prayed over them and healed them, which made everyone honor Paul and those with him greatly. And when the time came for them to set sail, three months later, they gave them what they needed of provisions and clothing.

28.8.1.en: God gives with the temptation the way of escape. After days of drifting at sea and the feeling of being lost, relief came from the face of the Lord and they were treated with great honor, and Paul the prisoner came into great glory and became a cause of kindness to those who held him captive. So if the affliction increases, continue your prayers to God, who is able not only to rescue you but to change the affliction into great blessings. And if the offenses directed at you increase and you are even exposed to death like Paul, God is able to deliver you and to make you a cause of blessing for all who offended you, like the soldiers who wanted to kill Paul. But what matters is that you keep your love for those who harm you and your faith in your mighty God.

28.9.0.en: Castor and Pollux: the names of two gods whom sailors believe guard their ships at sea.

28.9.1.en: After three months, they set sail from Malta and boarded a ship from Alexandria bearing the sign of Castor and Pollux. The ship had been anchored at the island during the winter, in which it is preferable not to travel.

28.10.0.en: The ship arrived at Syracuse, which is the capital of the island of Sicily and lies about eighty miles from Malta, and they stayed there three days.

28.11.0.en: The ship's sailors were compelled to go around in order to take advantage of the thrust of the wind, since it was contrary to their direction, so they arrived at Rhegium, a port in southern Italy. And after a day a south wind blew and drove them to Puteoli in western Italy.

28.12.0.en: In the city of Puteoli there were some Christians, so they received the ship's passengers as guests for a week, and perhaps it was an opportunity for Paul to reassure them, preach to them, and strengthen their faith. Then they moved on to Rome, which is about 140 miles from there.

28.13.0.en: Appii Forum: a market on the road between Puteoli and Rome, a hundred miles from Puteoli and forty miles from Rome. It is a place where people buy their needs, and so journeys stop there.

28.13.1.en: The Three Taverns: that is, three inns on the road to Rome after Appii Forum, about ten miles from Rome, and this place is considered a resting place for travelers.

28.13.2.en: A group of the Christians of Rome came out to meet them as far as the region of Appii Forum and the Three Taverns. Paul rejoiced at this reception and took courage, in return for what he had faced of imprisonment, trials, and shipwreck.

28.14.0.en: Dwelt by himself: Roman law allowed some prisoners of good repute to live in private houses of their own which they rented and not leave them, and they would be under guard, bound with chains to the soldiers guarding them.

28.14.1.en: When the journey reached Rome, Julius, the centurion, delivered the prisoners to the captain of the camp, and testified to Paul's greatness, his wisdom, and the power of his God, and also gave him Festus' letter, which testifies to the soundness of Paul's position, so the captain of the camp permitted him to dwell in a private house with the soldiers responsible for guarding him. Six soldiers were changed daily to guard Paul, each one's guard lasting four hours, during which he would be bound by a chain to Paul's hand.

28.14.2.en: God is able to give you favor in the eyes of those around you so that you may complete your spiritual striving and your service. So thank Him at all times, and make use of the blessings He bestows on you in order to draw near to Him.

28.15.0.en: After three days: from his arrival in Rome.

28.15.1.en: Paul hastened to begin preaching in Rome, so he sent and summoned the chief of the Jews to meet with them. At that time there were in Rome about sixty thousand Jews, who had seven synagogues and a quarter of their own. He told them that he was their brother and had done nothing against the Jews in Jerusalem or against the worship and the customs of the fathers, but that the Jews of Jerusalem had seized him and delivered him to the Romans, so he had come to Rome in bonds.

28.16.0.en: Paul told the chief of the Jews that the Romans had examined him and found him innocent, not deserving death on any account, and wished to release him.

28.17.0.en: The Jews opposed Paul and tried to kill him, so he was compelled to appeal his case to Caesar's court, because he was a Roman and had this right. In this he did not wish to bring his people to trial, but to stop the evil of these obstinate ones.

28.18.0.en: For this reason, Paul hastened to meet with the Jews of Rome, to see them and to confirm to them his message, from which it would become clear to them that the reason for his imprisonment is his faith in the Messiah, who is the hope of every Jew.

28.19.0.en: Since the time of Paul's voyage was in winter, when all the ships that carry news to other lands stop, they told him that nothing had yet reached them about him or his case from the Jews of Jerusalem.

28.20.1.en: The Jews asked him to set before them what he preaches, since they know that Christianity faces opposition everywhere.

28.21.0.en: A day was appointed for the meeting and a large number of Jews came to Paul's house, and he preached to them the Kingdom, of which the Law and the prophets prophesied, with prophecies and types concerning the Lord Jesus. This exposition continued for a whole day from beginning to end.

28.22.0.en: In the end, some of them were convinced of what was said and others were not convinced.

28.23.0.en: The Jews departed: divided among themselves, especially since Paul had ended his speech with what is in Isaiah (6:9-10) of God's words to him, declaring that the Jews would not hear the voice of God and would not discern it because of their obstinacy and the extreme hardness of their hearts, as if they feared hearing and understanding and returning to God to enjoy His blessings.

28.24.0.en: The salvation of God: the preaching of Christ the Savior.

28.24.1.en: Paul made clear to the Jews that God had sent the good news to the Gentiles, and that they would receive this preaching which the Jews themselves reject.

28.25.0.en: The Jews departed from Paul, and continued among themselves discussing what they had heard from Paul.

28.26.0.en: Paul continued preaching for two whole years (AD 61, 62) in Rome, settled in a house he had rented, and during them he preached to many Jews and Gentiles, among them Onesimus, the slave of Philemon (Phlm 10), who had come as a fugitive from his master who lived in Colossae. In it he sent the four prison epistles, to Philippi, Colossae, Ephesus, and Philemon. With him during them were Timothy, Luke the Evangelist, Epaphroditus, Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Tychicus, Justus, and Demas, as appears from the beginning and the end of the prison epistles.

28.27.0.en: Paul continued preaching Christ and the Kingdom without hindrance from the Romans, because they considered Christianity a sect of Judaism. Then they began their persecution of Christianity two years later, that is, in AD 64, after the Emperor Nero burned Rome and accused the Christians of it.

28.27.1.en: Paul preached while awaiting his trial without despair, anxiety, or complaint. God had permitted afflictions and prison for Paul, but He was with him, so he preached during them until he reached Rome and preached there. Thus the Book of Acts ends with the preaching reaching Rome, the capital of the empire, that is, the end of the earth, as Christ promised His disciples (ch. 1:8). After Paul's release from his first imprisonment in Rome, which is mentioned in this chapter, he preached in many places for five years. After that he was arrested and imprisoned in Rome for his second imprisonment, from which he sent his second epistle to Timothy, and then he was martyred in AD 68.

28.27.2.en: Do not waste your time on many things, so that you drift away from your goal, which is Christ. And let it not hinder you that some are not convinced by your words, but persevere in offering your love and your proclamation of Christ through all your life and your words, and God will support you and draw to Himself everyone who is ready to believe and to remain firm in the spiritual life because of you.
